content.thinking:
I need to be careful here — the cost figures were given to me, not derived by my own analysis, so I shouldn't present them as if I calculated them myself. I'll write the root cause, executive summary, and assumptions while referencing the incident window times factually, treating the impact numbers as externally measured rather than something I'm computing or estimating.

I also want to flag some open assumptions honestly: the leak hypothesis was only confirmed by the fact that a restart resolved things, without any heap dump or profiling to back it up, so an untracked change causing the issue hasn't really been ruled out. And the error-rate spike is being attributed to the same root cause, even though ClientDisconnected errors were already occurring before the onset — that link deserves scrutiny too.

assumptions: The memory leak is a diagnosis from metric and log shape (monotonic heap growth, flat traffic, no recorded change, recovery on restart); no heap dump or allocation profile was captured to prove it.

The change feed and flag-provider history were assumed complete for the windows queried. If an untracked config push, flag flip or deploy happened around 08:48Z, the alternative explanation - a newly enabled memory-hungry code path - has not been ruled out.

The elevated error rate is attributed to the same memory pressure, but the ClientDisconnected errors seen during the incident also appear before the onset, so some of the failures were pre-existing background noise rather than incident-caused.
Recovery is taken from the restart and the service returning to baseline on observation; no separate confirmation that heap growth has not resumed on the restarted process is included here.
The draft pull request is assumed to address the leak but was not reviewed, tested or merged as part of this incident.
input.executive_summary: On 24 September 2026 the online shop's account pages got progressively slower and a small share of requests failed. The problem began at about 08:51 UTC and the service was back to normal behaviour by 09:17 UTC. Shoppers loading account pages during that window saw slow responses, and a minority saw a failed page load; the great majority of requests still succeeded, and no data was lost. The cause was a background build-up of memory inside one of the shop's services, which gradually starved it of working room. The automated response system detected the alert, diagnosed the build-up, restarted the affected service, and confirmed it had returned to normal behaviour shortly after. A draft code change to address the underlying memory build-up has been opened for engineering review. Impact figures for this incident were measured separately from the shop's own traffic records and are reported there.
input.root_cause: A long-running io-shop process leaked memory: from ~08:48Z its heap climbed monotonically (~460MB toward ~1.38GB against a 2GiB limit) with request volume flat and no deploy, config or flag change in the retrieved windows, and the resulting GC pressure dragged p95/p99 latency up and pushed error rates above baseline until the process was restarted. The leak was inferred from the metric and log shape rather than from a heap profile; restarting the process cleared it, which is consistent with unreleased memory in the process itself.
